nameStory: Short-awn foxtail gets its name from its soft, fuzzy flower spike that looks remarkably like a fox's tail swishing in the breeze. The 'short-awn' part refers to the tiny bristle-like extensions on each flower that are shorter than those found on its cousin, meadow foxtail. When you see these delicate, bottle-brush shaped seed heads catching the morning light, you'll understand why early botanists thought of clever foxes!
description: Short-awn foxtail is a slender annual grass that grows in small clumps near water sources throughout New England. This delicate grass typically reaches 1-3 feet tall with narrow, soft green leaves and distinctive cylindrical flower spikes that resemble tiny bottlebrushes. The entire plant has a gentle, graceful appearance that sways easily in the slightest breeze. Despite being quite common across the Northern Hemisphere, it's surprisingly uncommon in New England, making it a special find for grass enthusiasts.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Soft, cylindrical spikes 2-4 inches long that feel fuzzy to the touch, resembling miniature bottlebrushes or fox tails. The pale green to purplish spikes are densely packed with tiny flowers that have very short bristles (awns).

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, flat blades that feel smooth and soft between your fingers. The leaves are typically 2-6 inches long with a distinctive boat-shaped tip and parallel veins running lengthwise.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small, loose tufts or clumps rather than spreading into dense mats. The stems are slender and often lean at angles, giving the plant a relaxed, informal appearance.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny, oval seeds that fall easily from the spike when ripe, often leaving behind the fuzzy appearance of the empty flower head. Seeds have a slight orange tint when mature.

habitat: Look for short-awn foxtail in wet, muddy areas near fresh water sources like pond edges, stream banks, ditches, and seasonal wetlands. It thrives in areas that experience periodic flooding or standing water, often growing alongside sedges, rushes, and other water-loving grasses. The plant prefers full sun to partial shade and rich, moist soils.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small tufts of narrow green leaves, beginning their rapid growth as soil moisture is highest.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time when the characteristic foxtail flower spikes appear and mature, typically from June through August.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and disperse, with the fuzzy flower heads becoming more obvious as seeds drop out, then the annual plants begin to decline.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely as this is an annual grass, leaving only seeds in the soil to germinate the following spring.

funFact: This humble grass is actually a world traveler that has managed to establish itself across three continents, yet in New England it's so uncommon that there have been only two documented observations - making it rarer here than some of our rarest wildflowers!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with meadow foxtail, but short-awn foxtail has much shorter bristles on its flower spike and grows in wetter areas. Memory trick: 'Short-awn likes to get its feet wet' - it's always near water, while meadow foxtail prefers drier grasslands.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the 'foxtail' name worry you - this gentle grass is completely unrelated to the dangerous foxtail grass seeds that can harm pets. Those problematic foxtails belong to different grass genera entirely and have much sharper, more aggressive seed structures.
compareHints: Short-awn foxtail differs from meadow foxtail by preferring wet habitats over dry meadows, having much shorter bristles (awns) on its flower spikes, and being an annual rather than perennial. The flower spikes of short-awn foxtail also tend to be more slender and delicate-looking compared to the robust, chunky spikes of meadow foxtail.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Meadow foxtail differs from its relative short-awn foxtail by being much larger and more robust overall.
